NPU engine#

The NPU engine is in progress: correctness first, speed next. Its kernels, built from source, match an fp64 reference on Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B and 4B. The layer kernel and lm head reach cosine similarity 0.9999 or better at every tested position, and greedy decoding matches the reference token for token. They are not merged into this repository yet. The release carries the NPU runtime, compiled into 1bit, and the npu backend of Lemonade's onebit recipe; until the kernels land, a release package serves GGUF models on HRX, not NPU models (Releases).

The NPU runtime and the NPU kernels are proprietary and closed source (Releases). They ship only as compiled binaries: the runtime is compiled into 1bit, and the kernels ship as compiled, encrypted artifacts that 1bit verifies and decrypts in memory at load (a wrong key fails cleanly, and nothing phones home). Their source, build and method are not in this repository or in any release. This page covers the public parts: the model format, how 1bit serve runs an NPU model, and how to build.

A model directory#

<model dir>/
  model.q4nx             weights (safetensors layout, Q4NX tiles: "Q4NX chunks" below)
  config.json            Hugging Face config: dimensions, rope_theta, eos_token_id
  tokenizer.json         Hugging Face tokenizer
  npu/                   the model's NPU kernels

1bit serve -m <model dir> serves such a directory on the NPU behind the OpenAI-compatible API (1bit serve); inside Lemonade, that is what its onebit backend runs (--onebit npu).

Q4NX chunks#

Q4NX is FastFlowLM's NPU model format (MIT), and its models on Hugging Face (FastFlowLM/*-NPU2) are Q4NX directories. A Q4NX weight is a grid of 32-row x 256-column tiles, one chunk each, row-major over the grid. The chunk kind is the last dimension of the tensor's shape: [tiles, 5120], or [tile rows, tile cols, chunk bytes] (npu/q4nx.h has the byte layouts).

Chunk Kind Weight Seen in
5120 B q4_1: bf16 scale and zero per 32 columns of a row code * scale + zero Qwen3, Llama, Gemma, Phi models
4736 B Q4_K: u8 scale and min per 32 columns, bf16 S, M per row S * scale * code + M * min Qwen3.5-4B projections
8704 B Q8: bf16 scale per 32 columns, int8 codes d * code Qwen3.5-4B lm_head and embedding

Q8 has two code layouts under the same chunk size. Qwen3.5-4B's lm_head (tied to the embedding) stores code (row r, column k) at byte k*32 + r. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B's Q8 tensors (untied lm_head, projections) store it at (r/16)*4096 + (k/32)*512 + (k%32)*16 + r%16. Both containers report flm_version 1.0.3, and neither carries metadata that tells them apart. Decoding tile (0, 0) of each lm_head and comparing with a GGUF of the same model gives correlation 0.9998 with the right layout and about 0.01 with the other. npu/q4nx decodes the first layout.

npu/q4nx.h decodes all three, and repacks Q4_K into q4_1 (exact apart from rounding S * scale and M * min to bf16), so code that reads q4_1 runs Q4_K weights unchanged. Q8 does not fit q4_1. tests/npu_q4nx_test.cpp checks the decoders bit for bit against reference decoders on real Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-0.6B tiles (committed in tests/golden/q4nx), and the repack against its rounding bound.

From a GGUF#

tools/gguf_to_q4nx.py pack <model.gguf> <out dir> --tokenizer <dir> writes a model directory's model.q4nx and config.json from a GGUF (qwen3 only for now), and copies tokenizer.json from --tokenizer. It writes every projection and lm_head as q4_1 tiles and the norms and embedding as bf16. A tied lm_head is made from token_embd.

GGUF type To q4_1 Error
Q4_0 scale d, zero -8d, codes unchanged bf16 rounding of scale and zero
Q4_1 scale d, zero m, codes unchanged bf16 rounding of scale and zero
Q4_K per 32-column sub-block: scale d*sc, zero -dmin*mn, codes unchanged (a Q4_K super-block is one tile row's 256 columns) bf16 rounding of scale and zero
Q5_K, Q6_K, Q8_0, F16, BF16, F32 dequantized, then min/max q4_1 per 32 columns lossy

tools/gguf_to_q4nx.py verify <model.gguf> <out dir> decodes every tensor it wrote and compares it with the GGUF, dequantized. For the exact types, every weight must lie within the bf16 rounding bound. The requantized tensors show their error.

On Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf (unsloth), all 311 tensors pass. The Q4_K tensors have 0 weights over the bound. The Q6_K tensors (half of v_proj and down_proj, and lm_head from the Q6_K embedding) requantize to cosine 0.9969 and relative RMS error 0.079. Served on the NPU, the repacked model decoded 24/24 greedy tokens the same as a CPU reference of the repacked weights, with every step's logits at cosine 0.99995 or better.

1bit serve -m <model.gguf> --device npu repacks a GGUF itself, caches the result under ~/.cache/1bit/q4nx/, and serves it. The repack runs the engine's own scripts/repack_gguf.py, which the package ships beside 1bit (scripts/, with its declared-scale guard; ONEBIT_Q4NX_REPACK overrides the path), so a packed install repacks too. It needs python3 with numpy and gguf, and FastFlowLM's Q4NX converter, which is not vendored: point ONEBIT_Q4NX_CONVERTER at a converter checkout (a ~/np-model-generic beside the engine or in the home directory is found without it). GGUFs of six architectures (Qwen2.5, Qwen3 MoE, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MiniCPM4/5, GLM-4.7-Flash) answer correctly this way, on a generic per-op path that is not yet fast (#179, #181, #209). On a release, GGUFs belong on HRX.

Declared scales are checked. The repack (scripts/repack_gguf.py) fails with rc=1 if the GGUF declares a known-critical scale-like value that the repacked config.json drops: embedding_scale, residual_scale, logit_scale, scale_emb, scale_depth, dim_model_base, final_logit_softcapping, attn_logit_softcapping. MiniCPM4-8B decoded punctuation soup because three of them were dropped, and no argmax-level check can see the third, which moves only the probabilities. Any other scale-like key (*scale*, *softcap*, *mup*) is warned about, not fatal. scripts/check_repack_config.py runs the same scan on its own, with a negative control.

A cached directory is checked again on every hit, with the same metadata-only scan, and it is rebuilt if the scan fails or if its repack-stamp.txt (converter path and commit, architecture, repack script) names a different converter than this build would use (repack_gguf.py --check-stamp <dir>: exit 0 current, 1 stale, 2 cannot tell). If the checker or the converter cannot be found, serve warns once per process and reuses the directory, so a missing script cannot stop serving. A Q4NX directory served as it is (1bit serve -m <Q4NX dir>), such as a published FastFlowLM model, is trusted as published. Its chunk layout can be checked first, without dequantizing anything: tools/check_q4nx_dir.py <dir> reads the container header only, names each quantized tensor's chunk kind, and refuses an unknown chunk size or a tensor shorter than its layout needs. It cannot tell the two Q8 layouts apart ("Q4NX chunks", above), because the container does not record which one it holds.

Cross-check against the official converter#

ROCm's FLM_Q4NX_Converter (convert.py) is the official gguf → Q4NX converter, and since 2026-10 it is public and Apache-2.0; scripts/repack_gguf.py already drives it for the 1bit serve --device npu repack path. It was run against tools/gguf_to_q4nx.py on the same GGUF (Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_0ctl.gguf, qwen3, 311 tensors: 196 Q4_0 projections, Q8_0 embedding and lm_head, F32 norms) and both containers were byte-compared tile by tile (tools/q4nx_diff.py compare) and decoded back against the GGUF (tools/q4nx_diff.py decode). Tensors: 114 of 311 byte-identical (the bf16 norms and embedding), 197 differ.

The container format is the same; the payload is not. Same tensor names, dtypes (I8 / BF16), shapes and tile geometry (32x256, 5120 B = 512 scale + 512 min + 4096 codes), and model.q4nx headers differ only by this engine's 104-byte __metadata__ block — the official output's header is byte-size-identical to the shipped Qwen3-0.6B-NPU2 container. The tiles differ because the two encodings are different, both exactly:

this engine (npu/q4nx.cpp) official converter
Q4_0 zero-point in the min plane, -8d min plane is 0
Q4_0 codes unsigned q (0..15) signed q-8, nibble = q xor 8
code order in a tile [row-half(2)][group(8)][col-in-group(32)][row-pair(8)] (the 16-row split the kernel walks) plain column major [col(256)][row-pair(16)]

Measured, per tensor, against the GGUF as ground truth: 196/196 Q4_0 tensors exact (0.0 error) under each file's own decoder — so both converters are correct — and 0/197 exact when one is read with the other's decoder (worst error 2.8-3.0). The scale planes of all 53 760 Q4_0 tiles are byte-identical; every min byte and every code byte differs. A container written by one converter must not be fed to the other's decoder: this engine's ELF route decodes the former layout only, which is also why npu/model.cpp and tools/q4nx_to_gguf.py refuse a container whose provenance they cannot establish.

The one place both are lossy is the Q8_0 lm_head: neither keeps it at 8 bits, both requantize to a 5120-byte tile. This engine's packer does it deliberately per 32 columns (max error 1.65e-2, rms 2.28e-3 against the source); the official path runs the 8-bit codes through its 4-bit packer (max error 3.23e-1, rms 2.94e-2, ~13x worse).

Two divergences worth knowing before packing a GDN model: the official qwen3.5_* configs carry a per-tensor dtype table (Q4_K default, ssm_out_proj Q4_K, alpha/beta Q8_0, lm_head Q8_0, norms BF16), prefill-mode .bf16 twins for ssm_alpha_proj/ssm_beta_proj, an (q g) -> (g q) reorder with q=2 for ssm_a and ssm_dt.bias, parallel_size 32 and keep_block_in_2D true. tools/gguf_to_q4nx.py has none of that (it is qwen3-only, parallel_size 16 semantics), so a hybrid-GDN model — including this engine's 27B — cannot be packed by it yet; the official configs are carried as data in configs/q4nx/ so that gap is described rather than guessed at.

tools/gguf_to_q4nx.py pack now also looks for tokenizer.json beside the GGUF when --tokenizer is omitted, and warns loudly when it is still missing: a directory without it is not servable, and the tool used to report success anyway.

Serving#

The 1bit NPU engine runs the model on the XDNA 2 NPU. With a release package that carries the NPU kernels (dense Qwen3: 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B):

./1bit serve -m <Qwen3 NPU model dir> --port 8000

In Lemonade, the onebit recipe's npu backend serves the same directories (--onebit npu). The model directory holds the weights only; the kernels ship inside the package.

Sealed kernel sets: the manifest is what says a set is ours#

A set ships as <set>/layout.json, <set>/layer1_*/layer1.elf (each 1BPKCRYP ciphertext, opened in memory by the loader with the kernel key) and two more files: manifest.json, which lists every file the set carries with the sha256 of its ciphertext, and manifest.sig, an Ed25519 signature over the manifest's exact bytes made with the release signing key. Sealing on its own is confidentiality only: a set re-sealed by another key, or swapped for a different set that also decrypts, would be indistinguishable from ours. The signature covers the manifest, the manifest's digests cover the ciphertext files, and the release public key never leaves the loader.

tools/seal_manifest.py is the public half: write <set> --key <release key> emits both files, check <set> proves the manifest lists exactly the set's files with their sha256 (no key needed), and verify <set> --pub <release public key> proves the signature too. scripts/package-linux.sh refuses to pack a set without them, scripts/weekly.sh's package_checks refuses a tarball whose sets do not match their manifests (ONEBIT_SEAL_PUB=<release public key> also verifies the signatures there), and 1bit-release-check's sealed/sealed-sig rows prove the same on the stick (the signature where the image has an interpreter and the key). The loader-side requirement, ONEBIT_KCRYPT_REQUIRE_MANIFEST=1 beside ONEBIT_KCRYPT_REQUIRE_SEALED, is read by the private NPU runtime and lands with the pin that makes it honour one - engine #574.

Dense Qwen3, checked on the NPU#

All three dense Qwen3 models run on the NPU from a sealed kernel set, and each one passes the hardware gate's npu phase (Hardware gate): greedy decoding token for token against an independent fp64 reference over a short prompt and teacher-forced steps, the 64-position build, the prompt prefill, and byte-identical output when the run is repeated, with the phase's speed floor met. Each is a catalogue entry in Lemonade, and each answers there:

Model npu phase Decode tok/s Lemonade entry chat-short tok/s
Qwen3-0.6B PASS 90.7 Qwen3-0.6B-NPU-1bit 93.7
Qwen3-1.7B PASS 39.5 Qwen3-1.7B-NPU-1bit 41.3
Qwen3-4B PASS 16.8 Qwen3-4B-NPU-1bit 17.7

Measured on Strix Halo, 90 W cap, PCM pad (23 Oct). Decode tok/s is the gate phase's own 64-position run; the phase's speed floor is set per model, 60 tok/s at 0.6B and scaled down by the model's size for the two larger ones. chat-short is lemonade bench --scenarios chat-short --runs 3 (mean of three runs, 0 failed) on a private server with one model loaded at a time. The checker that runs the phase is private, like the kernels it runs.

  • Tokenizer: npu/tokenizer.cpp reads tokenizer.json directly (PCRE2 for the pre-tokenizer regex). Added tokens with special: false, such as Qwen3's <think> and </think>, stay whole, as Hugging Face tokenizers does. tests/data/qwen3_tokenizer_golden.json holds 14 cases encoded by tokenizers 0.23.1, and all 14 match, ids and round trip.
  • Endpoints: /v1/health (503 while loading), /v1/models, /v1/chat/completions (streaming or not) and /v1/completions.
  • Prompt: ChatML, Qwen2/Qwen3's template for text messages.
  • Decoding: greedy, with a 1.1 repetition penalty over the last 64 ids by default. repetition_penalty in the request overrides it, and 1 gives plain greedy.
  • One request at a time: the model has one KV cache.
  • Repeatable: every generation starts from a zeroed KV cache (#400), so identical greedy requests give identical text, whatever ran before them.

The dense FFN tail cache (hybrid GDN models)#

On a GDN model the guard that skips the per-token Q4NX dequant in step() can never fire (dense_weights_cached requires lin_kd_ == 0, and lin_kd_ is model-level), so a hybrid model re-dequantised each layer's 17408-wide dense FFN tail on every token even after those weights were packed on the device. ffn_tail_cached() (npu/forward/src/q4nx_forward.cpp) closes that: once a layer's packed gate/up/down BOs are resident, the f32 wg_/wu_/wd_ buffers are no longer read, so the reload is skipped. It is on by default for a GDN model on the NPU route, when the packed weight cache is on, the run is not NPU_INFER_HOST_GEMM, and the tail is at least 256 MB per layer (the size guard; below that the reload is too small to be worth a behaviour change). NPU_FFN_CACHE=0 or =1 forces it either way, and the resolved state is logged once as [ffn] dense-tail cache on|off (default|NPU_FFN_CACHE; lin_kd=… IM=… H=…). On Qwen3.8-27B-NPU2 an interleaved 5-round A/B (~/lb/587-cache-20261030) measured an 8-token request at 104.5 s against 117.4 s (−11%), CPU per token 22.9 s against 63.3 s (−64%), same text in every arm.

Sampling and structured output#

1bit serve -m <NPU model dir> --device npu serves through 1bit forward-serve (app/forward_serve.cpp) in the same process. Every field below is optional, and the answer is greedy when none of them is sent, so a client written before them gets the same text it got before.

Request field Meaning
temperature 0 or absent decodes greedily (argmax); above 0 divides the logits before the draw
top_k keep the k highest logits; 0 or absent keeps all of them
top_p nucleus sampling, 1 or absent keeps all of them (min_keep candidates always stay)
seed the same seed and the same request give the same text; absent or -1 seeds from the clock
stop up to 4 strings: generation stops before the first match, and the tail is held back so a stop split across two tokens still matches
grammar a GBNF grammar in llama.cpp's format (third_party/llama.cpp/grammars/*.gbnf) the answer cannot leave
response_format {"type": "json_object"} constrains the answer to JSON; {"type": "json_schema"} is a 400

A field the route cannot honour is a 400 whose error.message says why ("json_schema needs a schema-to-GBNF converter this route does not have", "gbnf: unterminated literal at line 1"), never a silently ignored key. finish_reason is length when max_tokens ran out, and stop for an end-of-sequence token, a stop sequence or a grammar that allows nothing more.

The sampler is llama.cpp's, without llama.cpp: app/npu_sampling.h repeats the semantics of third_party/llama.cpp/src/llama-sampler.cpp (top_k, then top_p, then temperature, then the cumulative-sum draw that common/sampling.cpp's chain ends with) over the raw logits this route has, because llama.cpp's sampler needs a llama_context and a llama_vocab and the forward has neither. The grammar (app/npu_grammar.h) is the same rule model - one flat element vector per rule, ALT/END between alternatives - as a byte-level pushdown automaton: a token is only sampled when its decoded text leaves the grammar alive, which is checked per token against the byte ranges the grammar can continue with. Both headers are device-free, and tests/npu_sampling_test.cpp runs the sampler, the parser, the JSON grammar and the request parser in CI without a model or an NPU.

$ curl -sS localhost:8000/v1/completions -d '{"prompt": "The capital of France is", "max_tokens": 16,
    "grammar": "root ::= \" Paris\" | \" Lyon\" | \" Marseille\""}'
{"choices":[{"finish_reason":"length","index":0,"text":" Paris"},...]}

Two streams on one NPU#

One process owns the NPU by default: it takes an exclusive flock on /tmp/1bit-npu-device.lock for its lifetime (app/npu_device_lock.h), so a second serve of the NPU route waits instead of contending. That is a policy, not a hardware limit -- the driver advertises 16 hardware contexts on this part (hwctx_limit = 16, drivers/accel/amdxdna/npu4_regs.c) and only refuses the 17th -- and the policy stays the default because a second stream buys much less than 2x:

  • The DMA engine is shared. Decode reads the model's int8 weights once per token (~24.3 GB at ~2.2 GB/s effective on the 27B, engine#587); two streams split that bandwidth instead of doubling it.
  • The weights are not shared. Each stream packs its own copy of every layer's weight BO from the model file, plus its own KV cache and scratch, so N streams cost N x the model's device footprint. The NPU's memory is the box's own LPDDR5X, the same pool the CPU and the iGPU draw from, so two 27B streams do not fit.

With that said, two streams do run, and the option is what says you meant it:

# stream 1 of 2, then stream 2 of 2, in two shells (different ports, same model)
./1bit serve -m <NPU model dir> --device npu --npu-streams 2 --port 8000
./1bit serve -m <NPU model dir> --device npu --npu-streams 2 --port 8001

--npu-streams N (1..16, default 1) is forward-serve's flag too: N = 1 keeps the exclusive lock, N >= 2 takes a shared lock, so the opted-in streams co-exist while any exclusive holder -- an unflagged 1bit serve, the per-process ELF runner (npu_engine_universal), another build's serve -- still keeps them all out, in either order, because they share one file and one flock(2).

The lock is one file and one protocol, across runtimes, and it is advisory -- that is what makes it usable beside another NPU engine, and what its limits are:

  • Path and modes. /tmp/1bit-npu-device.lock, created 0644 if absent, flock(2) (not fcntl) so it works across processes, users and runtimes on the box. LOCK_SH = "I am one of N streams, do not wait for other shared holders"; LOCK_EX = "I want the device to myself". A holder keeps its fd open for the life of the process; closing or exiting releases it. LOCK_EX and LOCK_SH never overlap, in either order, on one file.
  • Who may take what. Anything that honours the file interlocks with us: our serves (--npu-streams decides which mode), the ELF runner (LOCK_EX, always). A foreign NPU runtime -- Lemonade's ryzenai-llm backend on Windows, an ONNX session, a benchmark -- may take LOCK_EX to keep us out, or LOCK_SH to be one of the streams. Nothing forces it: a runtime that ignores the file is not slowed, not blocked and not detected.
  • What happens when the other engine ignores it. A runtime that skips the file is not blocked and not detected, so it shares the device exactly the way a co-ordinated second engine does — and that cost is measured: two engines on the shared lock lose 59 % of their aggregate throughput (the table below). The failure mode is slow, not wrong; there is no run on this box that measures an unco-ordinated second engine apart from that, so nothing more specific is claimed here.

Partitioning, and what it would take. Two whole-array streams share one DMA engine, so they serialise; the September prototype that scaled (~100 % each) did it by giving each stream a disjoint half of the columns, which halves per-stream weight reuse, and its xclbin pair is ABI-stale at this pin, so nothing in this tree can select a column split today: both of our instances run whole-array. What each engine costs is therefore the whole model per stream -- one hwctx and one complete copy of the weight BOs, plus its own KV cache and scratch, and the device's hwctx limit is 16. The accounting per engine is: streams x (weights + KV + scratch) must fit in the NPU's share of the box's LPDDR5X alongside whatever the other engine has already allocated, and both engines pull from the same DMA bandwidth. Two different models resident at once (the reason the second engine exists) is therefore bounded by memory first, not by hwctx: see the table below.

A model directory repacked from an FLM pack still carries FLM's own parameter map and version in config.json -- for Qwen3-0.6B, addr_qk 9216, addr_kv 33792, addr_kk 45056, addr_l_begin_mha 53760, addr_l_end_mha 25088, plus flm_version 0.9.22. Those are offsets into FLM's program layout for the AIE programs that live in the FLM install, not a description of this engine's memory: this route reads only the geometry keys (hidden_size, num_hidden_layers, num_attention_heads, num_key_value_heads, intermediate_size, vocab_size, head_dim) and finds its own full ELFs under --kernels, which is why a model directory's npu/ subdirectory is empty on purpose and why addr_* must not be used to reason about what this engine allocates.

What it measures. max_tokens 8, temperature 0, three reps per arm with rep 1 dropped as warm-up (the first request after a load is ~2x the steady state), wall clock per request, each model measured alone with the other not even loaded (strixhalo 2026-10-30, engine 38e29a2, binary b78868c, kernels ~/lb/lfm2-npu/kernels_m16, run ~/lb/612-npu-streams-20261030T112326Z):

run solo both at once per stream aggregate
Qwen3-0.6B + Qwen3-4B, --npu-streams 2 (b78868c, 2026-10-30) 5.79 s / 25.08 s 16.99 s / 35.61 s 34.1 % / 70.4 % 0.41x

That row is the one the second engine exists for: two different models resident at once, each keeping its own weights and its own hwctx, both answering, with no lock bypass. Throughput gets worse -- 0.41x, i.e. running the two back to back is 2.4x faster than running them together -- because two whole-array streams share one DMA engine: the per-token times add up (0.72 + 3.13 s solo per token = 3.85 s; concurrent rounds take 4.45 s) plus about 16 % of handoff overhead. The small model pays most (34 % of solo) because it is latency-bound; the 4B keeps 70 % because its token cost is its own 3.3 GB weight stream, which it would have spent anyway.

So co-residency buys availability, not throughput: each model keeps answering while the other is loaded, instead of a 25-30 s reload. For a short answer, reloading still beats sharing the device -- that is the trade, and it is why the exclusive default stays.

tests/npu_device_lock_test.cpp (ctest npu_device_lock, in CI) proves the lock discipline without a device: exclusive excludes everything, three shared streams co-exist, and an exclusive waits for the last one to go.

The row this exists for. On Linux the two engines are two instances of this runtime on two different models at the same time -- "all NPU models at once" -- and that is what tools/showcase-612-npu-streams.sh measures with MODEL and MODEL_B (default Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-4B, whose kernel sets are on this box): each model solo, then both at once, three reps, every number stamped with the build that produced it.

Add-on routes#

The engine keeps a hook for closed-source NPU add-ons (npu/private_route.h). Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (model_type qwen3_5_moe) runs on the NPU through one, experimentally; it is not in this repository and not in a release.

  • -DONEBIT_NPU_PRIVATE=<add-on checkout> (with -DONEBIT_NPU=ON) builds that checkout's addons/ into 1bit. It must define the target onebit_npu_private, which holds register_private_addon(); 1bit calls it at startup.
  • The add-on registers a route per model_type (whether it can serve a directory, and a session that generates from token ids) and may register 1bit subcommands. 1bit serve uses the route for that model type; --npu-opt KEY=VALUE passes options through to it.
  • A route can be optional: an opt-in route for a model_type the engine also serves. When it declines a directory (its unavailable() gives a reason), the engine serves the directory exactly as it would without the add-on.
  • Without the add-on, 1bit serve -m <35B dir> --device npu exits saying the route is not part of this build.

An add-on may also register an encoder for the Laya router (laya/encoder.h, Laya router). tests/npu_private_route_test.cpp (ctest npu_private_route, in CI) checks the registry and that message.

The runtime#

The engine reaches the NPU runtime only through its own public header, npu/npu_rt_api.h: the calls the engine's NPU code makes, each class an opaque handle. The runtime itself is not in this repository; a build from this repository alone has no NPU lane. ONEBIT_NPU=ON takes one of:

# the public binary drop (docs/releases.md, "The public binary drop")
cmake -B build -G Ninja -DONEBIT_HRX=ON -DONEBIT_NPU=ON -DONEBIT_BINARY_DROP=<drop dir or URL>
# a prebuilt runtime library that implements npu/npu_rt_api.h
cmake -B build -G Ninja -DONEBIT_NPU=ON -DONEBIT_NPU_RT_LIB=<path>/libnpu_rt_api.a
  • ONEBIT_NPU_HOST (the model reader, Q4NX, packing, the tokenizer) needs no runtime and builds everywhere, including public CI, where its tests run.
  • The release builds the runtime from a pinned commit named in config/npu-runtime.config (Releases).

The NPU needs the amdxdna kernel driver. third_party/xdna-driver pins upstream amd/xdna-driver as the driver version the engine is checked against (the kernel's own copy also works); nothing from the pin is built into or shipped with the release. .github/workflows/bump-xdna.yml moves the pin when run by hand, because a driver move means rebuilding the module on Strix Halo and checking the NPU there first.
